title: The Creator Guide to Leaving YouTube for a Platform You Own (2026)
html:
YouTube is the most generous of the big platforms and that is exactly what makes it hard to argue about. It genuinely built a middle class of full-time creators, it pays reliably, and the tooling is excellent. None of that changes the three things a channel owner cannot do: set their own rate, appeal a ranking decision, or take the channel with them.

This is the YouTube-specific companion to our guides on leaving TikTok and leaving Instagram. The pattern is the same everywhere. The specifics below are the ones that actually bite YouTubers.

The YouTube-specific problems

The 45% you never see

The Partner Programme splits ad revenue 55/45 in your favour on long-form, and 45/55 against you on Shorts after the music licensing pool is settled. Those are the published numbers and they are better than most competitors. They are also fixed: there is no tier where a channel large enough to matter negotiates its own rate, and the split has never moved in your direction.

The eligibility treadmill

Monetisation starts at 1,000 subscribers plus either 4,000 valid public watch hours in twelve months or 10 million valid Shorts views in ninety days. Clear it and you are not done — the thresholds must hold. A channel that dips below them loses monetisation, which means the worst month of your year is also the month the income stops.

Demonetisation you cannot predict

The yellow icon is the single most demoralising thing in the creator economy: an automated advertiser-suitability decision, applied to a video you have already made, with an appeal process that resolves after the traffic spike it was going to earn from has passed. Whole categories — news commentary, anything involving conflict, large parts of health, most of what people actually argue about — are structurally underpaid regardless of how carefully they are made.

Content ID and the strike system

A copyright claim can redirect a video's entire revenue to a third party, sometimes wrongly, and the burden of disputing it sits with you. Three strikes removes the channel. Not the video — the channel, the subscribers, the back catalogue and the income, all of it, on a decision you cannot see the reasoning behind.

You cannot take the subscribers

A million subscribers is a number in Google's database. There is no export, no direct line, and no portability. If the channel goes, the audience does not follow you — it simply stops being reachable.

What owning it instead looks like

On DeHub, the decentralised social network, an upload is minted on-chain to your wallet the moment you post. The ownership record exists independently of the platform, which is the practical difference between holding a deed and holding a tenancy. The feed is chronological and transparent, so nothing decides in private whether your work gets seen, and the code is open-source, so the rules cannot be quietly rewritten underneath you.

Up to 90%, published

DeHub commits up to 90% of ad revenue back to the ecosystem and the creators in it, and the figure is published rather than inferred from a dashboard. Against a 55% long-form split — or the effective 45% on Shorts — that is not a marginal improvement in the same game. It is a different arrangement.

No suitability lottery

Nothing here routes your revenue through an automated advertiser-suitability model. Uploads can be free, pay-per-view, or token-gated, so a video that no advertiser wants to sit beside can still be the best-paid thing you publish — because the viewer pays for it directly rather than an ad network deciding whether it deserves to exist.

Subscriptions that resell

DeHub subscriptions are minted on-chain and are tradable, and the original creator earns a royalty when one is resold. A membership becomes an asset with a life after its first sale instead of a monthly charge that ends when someone cancels. Our explainer on tokenised subscriptions walks through how the royalty flows back.

Watch-to-earn, for the long-form problem

Retention is the whole game on long-form and the thing YouTube rewards most opaquely. DeHub lets you attach watch-to-earn bounties that pay viewers in crypto for genuinely watching, which buys real attention rather than the impressions that inflate a view count without moving anything. Start with what watch-to-earn is if the model is new.

Earnings settle in DHB, primarily on Base, an Ethereum Layer 2, with contracts on BNB Chain and Polygon. It trades on decentralised exchanges and on Coinbase and is listed on CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap, so what you earn is liquid rather than stuck inside one company's ledger.

Live, without the middleman

If you stream, DeHub's live streaming runs on Livepeer, has scaled past 50,000 concurrent viewers, and tips land directly rather than being clipped on the way through. Our Web3 live streaming guide compares that against the incumbents properly.

How to migrate a YouTube channel without losing it

The mistake is treating this as a switch. It is a hedge.

  1. Claim your handle. Free, first-come, and much less awkward to do before you need it.
  2. Mirror your back catalogue. Long-form archives are the easiest thing in the world to double-post, and they populate a new home instantly.
  3. Move the videos YouTube punishes. Every channel has them: the essay that got a yellow icon, the topic the suitability model dislikes, the thing you did not upload because you knew it would not pay. That is your differentiated library and it belongs where it can earn.
  4. Use the end screen and the description. The two places a YouTube viewer is already looking for somewhere else to go.
  5. Turn the money on early. Set up subscriptions and revenue share while your YouTube traffic is healthy, not after a strike.

Keep YouTube for discovery. It is superb at it. Just stop letting one company hold the deed, the rate card and the appeal process all at once.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best YouTube alternative for creators in 2026?

If you want the same product with a different logo, several exist, and every one of them keeps the same arrangement — they host, they rank, they set the split. If you want the split published and the ownership recorded to your wallet, that is a structurally different platform, which is where DeHub sits.

How much does YouTube actually pay?

The Partner Programme pays 55% of long-form ad revenue and 45% on Shorts after music licensing. What that translates to per thousand views depends on your niche, your audience's location and the advertiser demand in your category, which is why RPM figures vary by an order of magnitude between channels of identical size.

Can I move my subscribers off YouTube?

Not directly — there is no export and no messaging path. You convert them, over time, by consistently pointing at somewhere else and giving them a reason to go. Assume most will not, and plan around the ones who do.

Will I lose my YouTube channel by cross-posting?

No. Nothing in YouTube's terms prevents publishing the same work elsewhere, and mirroring is what most full-time creators already do across platforms. Keep YouTube running; the point is to stop depending on it exclusively.

Does DeHub work for long-form video, or just short clips?

Both. The platform carries long-form video, shorts, music, live streaming, images and text, and the monetisation options — free, pay-per-view, token-gated, watch-to-earn — apply per upload regardless of length.
